questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Federal examiners at the registration desk
questions.learningObjective: identify the obstacle the 1965 voting statute was built to remove
questions.stem: A 1965 statute allowed the national government to send its own examiners into a county where local registrars had refused to register Black applicants, and the federal list counted. What problem did that provision attack?

options.text: Local officials could keep voters off the roll by controlling it

options.misconception: reduces examiners to assistance at the polls
options.text: Voters needed help completing a printed form at the polls

options.misconception: explains the statute as a matter of funding
options.text: States lacked the money to pay for that year's elections

options.misconception: credits a partisan agreement on ballots
options.text: The two major parties had agreed to stop counting by race

questions.explanation: If the person deciding who registers is the person the law is meant to check, a barrier will be used, so the statute moved the deciding hand to an official whose list could be compared against the law itself. The tempting answer makes the examiners a convenience, but the provision answered a question of control over the roll, not a shortage of form-fillers or of money.
questions.hint: Who decides who appears on the roll of voters?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze what a change in registration rates reveals about the barrier
questions.stem: A county report shows 14 percent of eligible Black residents registered in 1963, then 71 percent two years after federal examiners began working there, while the white rate barely moved. Which conclusion does that change support?

options.text: The barrier was control of the roll, not unwillingness to vote

options.misconception: credits examiners with publicizing the vote
options.text: Voters had stayed away until examiners told them about it

options.misconception: misreads examiners as transportation providers
options.text: The examiners carried voters to the polling places themselves

options.misconception: attributes the change to a local statute
options.text: The county had adopted a civil rights statute on its own

questions.explanation: A rate that roughly quintupled in two years, while the white rate held steady, points to a barrier placed on one side of the process rather than to a general change of mind among voters, and the name on the roll is what an outside official's decision produced. The tempting answer credits publicity, but publicity had been available for decades without changing who got registered; what changed was who decided.
questions.hint: Which group moved, and what else stayed put?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify why an amendment was required to remove a voting tax
questions.stem: The poll tax fell hardest on the poorest voters and was collected at the ballot box, and states had written it into their own constitutions. What did the 1964 amendment have to do about it?

options.text: It removed a tax on voting that a state constitution had allowed

options.misconception: authorizes a federal poll tax
options.text: It gave the national government power to set a poll tax

options.misconception: invents a national election day
options.text: It required all states to hold elections on one day

options.misconception: confuses the poll tax with property limits
options.text: It ended any property holding rule for local voting

questions.explanation: Because the charge was written into a state constitution, a law passed by the national legislature could not repeal it, and that is why the change required the harder instrument of an amendment rather than ordinary legislation. The tempting answer reverses the direction of authority, crediting Congress with a tax power it did not gain; the amendment removed a tax rather than creating one.
questions.hint: What would a statute have had to repeal first?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze why discrimination in housing needed a new legal mechanism
questions.stem: By the late 1960s agents in some cities said a seller's preference out loud and steered buyers away from particular blocks, so the discrimination settled into the asking price of land. What did the housing law do about that?

options.text: It made racial steering a violation wherever housing is sold

options.misconception: invents a quota for sellers
options.text: It required sellers to offer homes to buyers in strict rotation

options.misconception: makes the statute a price control
options.text: It set the price that every home in a neighborhood must carry

options.misconception: reads the statute as a construction mandate
options.text: It asked municipalities to build more housing for large families

questions.explanation: Once a price is quoted to a buyer on the basis of who lives next door, the discrimination happens in a contract between private parties with no public building involved, so the law had to reach the people who quoted the price rather than the owners of the land. The tempting answer makes the statute a price or quota rule, which is a different mechanism; what it created was a wrong attached to a transaction and answerable in court.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify what the 1968 school ruling required of a district
questions.stem: A 1968 ruling rejected a plan promising desegregation at a pace the court called deliberately slow, and said the delay had no constitutional justification. What did that ruling require of the district?

options.text: An end to the delay, judged by present conditions

options.misconception: credits the ruling with fresh litigation
options.text: A new court order, because the first was left unexecuted

options.misconception: suggests the court ordered school closure
options.text: The closing of the schools until a plan was approved

options.misconception: turns the ruling into an award of damages
options.text: Payment of damages to the families whose children sat out

questions.explanation: The court's point was that time passing is not itself a reason to delay, so a district's slow plan could not be renewed on the ground that it was still being carried out. The tempting answer invents a new proceeding, but the case turned on whether the existing order had been honored, which made the pace of that plan the whole question.
questions.hint: Is a promise to act later a remedy?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a remedy had to be allowed to cross a district boundary
questions.stem: One district argued that a remedy had to stay inside its own lines, while the reviewing court approved busing that carried children across a district boundary. What was the court's reasoning?

options.text: Segregation was a pattern made across districts, not inside one

options.misconception: claims districts were stripped of their authority
options.text: Districts lost their school authority entirely after the ruling

options.misconception: makes busing the exclusive remedy
options.text: Busing was the only remedy the court would ever consider

options.misconception: recasts the ruling as an interstate agreement
options.text: The decision was a treaty approved in each neighboring state

questions.explanation: Districts had been drawn along lines that already separated children by race, so a remedy confined to one district would have had to accept the very pattern it was meant to break, which is why the court allowed students to be carried across the boundary. The tempting answer makes the ruling exclusive or sweeping, but it also set a limit on how far a remedy could travel while letting it cross a line.
questions.hint: Were the district lines drawn before or after the separation?

questions.learningObjective: analyze the authority a court exercised over a federal agency
questions.stem: A court found that a federal housing program had steered families into the city while the suburbs kept their own standards, and it ordered the agency to act on a plan reaching beyond the city it governed. What made that order possible?

options.text: A court's authority over a federal agency is not bounded by a city line

options.misconception: grants courts a general tax power
options.text: A federal court may order any local government to raise its taxes

options.misconception: claims the statute covered suburban housing
options.text: The agency's own statute had brought suburbs under federal power

options.misconception: claims congress delegated boundary redrawing
options.text: Congress had authorized courts to redraw the city boundaries

questions.explanation: The remedy failed wherever the agency could hold the families inside a jurisdiction that resisted, so the order had to reach the agency's own conduct past that line, and a federal court's power over a federal officer is what made it possible. The tempting answer turns the case into a general license over local government, when what the court exercised was authority over a federal agency, which is why the suburbs' own choices were not directly commanded.

options.misconception: claims a repeal of northern segregation statutes
options.text: Northern states had repealed their school segregation laws by 1968

options.misconception: extends southern rulings to the north
options.text: Southern law had by then been struck down in both regions

options.misconception: claims a funding cutoff in the north
options.text: National school funds had been withdrawn from northern districts

questions.explanation: The report mattered because it located the problem where no statute existed to repeal, since the mechanism was residential choice compounded by lending and steering, which is why a law against segregation could reach the school door and not the neighborhood. questions.learningObjective: identify the reasoning behind required warnings during questioning
questions.stem: In 1966 a ruling held that a statement taken without warnings about the right to stay silent and to have counsel could not be used at trial. What was the reasoning behind the warnings?

options.text: Pressure while questioning can make an admission that is not a decision

options.misconception: requires proof that the statement was false
options.text: Every confession had been proved false by the accused at trial

options.misconception: claims the trial right already existed
options.text: The right to counsel had already been given at the trial itself

options.misconception: credits congress with the warning rule
options.text: Congress had ordered police to give the warnings in advance

questions.explanation: The court did not decide that people lie under questioning, but that a person held by officers has more reason to agree with them than to disagree, so the safeguards had to come before the statement rather than after it. The tempting answer demands proof that a statement was false, which would leave the confession standing whenever it seemed true; the rule concerned how the statement was obtained.

questions.learningObjective: analyze the reasoning behind a voting age no longer justified by its origin
questions.stem: For most of the country's history the voting age was set at twenty-one, a figure taken from a time when military service and household independence began there. What did the 1971 amendment do to that reasoning?

options.text: It lowered the age without claiming that competence had changed

options.misconception: claims the amendment raised the voting age
options.text: It raised the voting age to match the age of enlistment

options.misconception: invents a literacy test tied to age
options.text: It required a literacy test before anyone under twenty-five voted

options.misconception: makes the age a state choice
options.text: It left every state free to set its own voting age

questions.explanation: The figure twenty-one measured the dependencies of an earlier era, and the amendment's silence about competence shows the change was argued from the arbitrariness of an old number rather than from evidence about young people's judgment. The tempting answer invents a test, but the amendment removed a qualification and set one uniform age, because the old bar had been a leftover rather than a measurement.

questions.learningObjective: analyze what changed when the federal government became the payer
questions.stem: In 1965 the federal government took over payment for the hospital and medical care of the elderly and the poor, replacing rules that had let a hospital turn away a patient who could not pay. What changed in practice?

options.text: The price of care no longer followed what a patient could pay

options.misconception: invents a uniform national price schedule
options.text: Hospitals were told to charge every patient the same fixed price

options.misconception: invents uniform fees for physicians
options.text: Doctors were paid one identical fee for the same work everywhere

options.misconception: assumes unlimited choice of provider
options.text: Patients could now choose any hospital without any limit

questions.explanation: Payment follows ability to pay, so a program that pays on a patient's behalf changes what a hospital can afford to refuse, and that is why the poor and the elderly stopped being turned away at the door. The tempting answer turns a change in who pays into a change in price, but the amounts charged and the fee schedules were left to the ordinary machinery of medicine while the question of acceptance was settled.

questions.topic: The growing population of the elderly

questions.stem: A federal table gives the population over sixty-five at about twenty million in 1960, about thirty million in 1980, and about thirty-five million in 2000, while the cost of the program for the elderly grew faster than the general price level. What does that pairing support?

options.text: A rising number of older patients raised the demand to be covered

options.misconception: blames providers for the cost growth
options.text: Hospitals raised their prices because the program paid them well

options.misconception: attributes the growth to expanded benefits
options.text: The program covered more services each year, not more patients

options.misconception: makes physician supply the driver
options.text: The number of physicians rose faster than the number of patients

questions.explanation: A benefit that pays for treatment goes where the treated are, so a population that grew by half across the generation being insured could not be expected to produce costs flat in real terms, and the two series moving together is what the table shows. The tempting answer puts the growth on the price side, but the count of insured people is the quantity the program was built to serve and it moved on its own schedule.

options.misconception: claims federal aid abolished tuition
options.text: Federal money ended all tuition at the public universities

options.misconception: invents a merger requirement
options.text: Private colleges were required to merge with the new campuses

options.misconception: makes building a state duty under the statute
options.text: The statute required states to build schools in every county

questions.explanation: Higher education had been priced for people who could leave work and pay for four uninterrupted years, so opening campuses near where people lived changed who could finish a degree rather than merely how many seats existed. options.text: The cost of care moves to families who have no funds for it

options.misconception: assumes care costs vanish with the buildings
options.text: The cost disappears along with the wards and their buildings

options.misconception: claims federal custody took over
options.text: The released patients become wards of the federal government

options.misconception: assumes counties were ordered to build
options.text: Counties are directed to build new hospitals of their own

options.misconception: claims female schooling declined

options.misconception: lets courts expand the statute's grounds
options.text: State courts were permitted to add grounds of their own choosing

options.misconception: claims the original list was implied
options.text: The earlier statute had barred sex discrimination by implication

questions.explanation: A list of protected grounds is exactly as long as the law says it is, and no one outside the legislature could add to it, which is why the change required a second vote and why women in the covered jobs kept waiting for it. The tempting answer credits the courts with reading a ground into the list, but the original wording was explicit and a court's task was to enforce what the words said.
questions.hint: Who can add a word to a statutory list?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze what a change after repeal shows about the rules
questions.stem: One administration removed or weakened rules written by earlier ones, and firms in the affected trade reported that compliance costs fell and hiring rose. What does that sequence establish?

options.text: The rules had been costs that firms could be freed from

options.misconception: attributes the trade's fortunes to regulation
options.text: The trade had suffered a shortage of workers that rules caused

options.misconception: claims prices were legally fixed
options.text: Prices in the trade were already fixed by law before the repeal

options.misconception: credits new rules for the hiring
options.text: Hiring rose because fresh rules had just been written instead

questions.explanation: A rule that costs money and shows a measurable change when removed is evidence of a cost that existed, and a drop in compliance spending with a rise in hiring together say the two moved as a rule would move them. The tempting answer reverses the order, crediting new rules for an improvement that followed their repeal, when the sequence of events points the other way.
questions.hint: What changed first, the spending or the rule?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fewer earners in the same household
questions.learningObjective: evaluate how falling earners per household changed risk
questions.stem: Two households earn the same income, but in one a married couple earns it and in the other a single man does, and a job loss in the first leaves two earners while in the second it leaves none. What has changed?

options.text: Earners per household fell while average income held roughly steady

options.misconception: confuses income shares with saving rates
options.text: Households with two earners lost their share of national saving

options.misconception: attributes the difference to housing costs
options.text: The single-earner household spent more on rent than the couple did

options.misconception: claims a mass withdrawal from work
options.text: Married couples stopped contributing to the labor force after 1960

questions.explanation: Rising incomes alongside fewer earners per household mean a job lost now removes a larger share of what the family had, so the same rate of joblessness reached further into household budgets than it had a generation before, and that changed what families had reason to protect. The tempting answer finds the change in spending or saving habits, but the series that rose was participation, which is why one layoff hurt more.
questions.hint: Which of the two numbers rose over these decades?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The poverty count and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: analyze what the timing of a series change implies about its cause
questions.stem: Official counts put the share of people in poverty at about 22 percent in 1959, 12 percent in 1970, and 15 percent in 1980, while unemployment stayed low until 1974. What does the timing suggest?

options.text: The gains leaned on employment and reversed when employment fell

options.misconception: claims a permanent floor of twelve percent
options.text: The programs in place by 1970 fixed the number permanently at twelve

options.misconception: attributes the rise to a changed definition
options.text: The count rose after 1980 because the definition was widened

options.misconception: reports a continuous decline through the decade
options.text: Poverty fell every year between 1960 and 1980 without any pause

questions.explanation: The line fell steeply while work was available and turned upward once employment turned down, and that pattern fits an income that leans on jobs more than on transfers, since a program aimed at a share of the population can hold a floor but cannot replace a wage. The tempting answer makes the programs the whole explanation, which the later rise contradicts, because transfers were already in place when the number climbed again.
questions.hint: Compare the turn in the series with the turn in employment.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze how a change in grant form moved authority
questions.stem: A program that had sent money to cities with federal rules attached was later given as a lump sum with the recipient free to set its own priorities. Why did officials make that change?

options.text: Local officials resented the conditions and the federal oversight

options.misconception: blames the change on administrative speed
options.text: Cities had proved unable to spend money faster than rules allowed

options.misconception: claims the transfer was to the states
options.text: The legislature moved the program over to the state governments

options.misconception: explains the change as a budget shortage
options.text: The national government had run out of money for the purpose

questions.explanation: Conditions attached to a grant made the recipient an administrator of federal instructions, and officials who disliked that role could only escape it by taking money without conditions, so the change moved authority by moving the money. The tempting answer makes the shift a matter of speed, but nothing in the fiscal account required fewer rules; the alteration was over who decided what the money was for.
questions.hint: What did the conditions make the recipient become?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a quota defended by old reasons could not survive
questions.stem: The law of 1965 ended a quota system written to favor particular national origins more than forty years earlier, and it opened admission to people from countries previously excluded. What explains the change in the debate?

options.text: The old preferences rested on arguments that no longer held

options.misconception: blames the quotas on foreign governments
options.text: The earlier quotas had been set by foreign governments, not congress

options.misconception: invents a reciprocity requirement
options.text: The law required every nation to admit a share of americans

options.misconception: claims a court removed congressional power
options.text: A ruling in 1964 had barred congress from setting admissions

questions.explanation: A quota defended as a reflection of an era's national character cannot survive when the reasons given for it no longer describe the country, so the statute repealing it was also a statement about which reasons the government would accept in future, and the argument over admission returned at once on new grounds. The tempting answer removes the statute's own authority to set numbers, which is the power congress kept and used.
questions.hint: What happens to a rule when its old reasons stop applying?
